en.title: Nintendo adds three more NES games to Switch Online, bringing the total to 87 in the West
en.description: Ninja Gaiden 3, Ikari Warriors and RC Pro-Am 2 join the Nintendo Classics service
en.fullContent:
Ninja Gaiden 3, Ikari Warriors and RC Pro-Am 2 join the Nintendo Classics service

Nintendo has added three more NES games to the Nintendo Classics service on Switch Online.

Ninja Gaiden 3: The Ancient Ship of Doom, Ikari Warriors and RC Pro-Am 2 are now available to play via the NES app.

Originally only released in Japan and North America when it arrived on the NES in 1991, Ninja Gaiden 3 sees protagonist Ryu Hayabusa – framed for a murder he didn’t commit – learning of a CIA plan to create a race of super mutants by taking them from another dimension.

The first two games are already available on Switch Online, meaning the entire NES trilogy is now available.

Ikari Warriors is a vertically scrolling run and gun shooter starring a pair of commandos called Paul and Vince (it can be played solo or co-op). Gunning down enemies is naturally the aim, and players can occasionally jump into a tank for extra firepower.

en.title: 'The Drifter' Video Game Getting Movie Treatment At Sony Pictures
en.description: EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures and Story Kitchen have landed live-action feature film rights to the video game The Drifter. Story Kitchen’s Dmitri M. Joh...
en.fullContent:
EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures and Story Kitchen have landed live-action feature film rights to the video game The Drifter. Story Kitchen’s Dmitri M. Johnson and Michael Lawrence Goldberg will be producing with Timothy I. Stevenson and Elena Sandoval executive producing the project.

The Drifter is a pulpy adventure video game where, after witnessing a brutal murder and being drowned by high-tech soldiers, a nomadic drifter awakens finding himself fighting for survival and unraveling a dark conspiracy involving shadowy corporations and a madman’s obsession. It is developed and published by Australian independent game studio Powerhoof.

Following word that Story Kitchen and Sony had landed rights, sources say top writers and directors are already reaching out to sell their pitch. While studios across town are high on video game adaptations including Sony, who has Resident Evil bowing this month, its rare to see this much attention on a game that was independently put together and not coming from one of the top-tier companies.

The Drifter won Game of the Year at the 2025 Australian Game Developer Awards where it also won for Excellence in Visual Art, Excellence in Narrative and Excellence in Sound Design.

As for Story Kitchen, they’re no strangers to video game adaptations with a strong slate of upcoming projects that includes Tomb Raider projects for Prime Video and Netflix; Life is Strange, which is also at Prime Video; a Just Cause movie at Universal; and Sega’s 1990s classic Streets of Rage at Lionsgate among others.

Powerhoof is a two-person indie game studio founded by Dave Lloyd and Barney Cumming. Their first game was Crawl, a dungeon-crawler game where your friends control the monsters. They followed up with Regular Human Basketball, a multiplayer party-starter, and The Drifter.

en.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming world
en.description: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that nee...
en.fullContent:
As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining

Predictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last week was a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to data collated by Eurogamer, more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention.

Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon.

I hope I’m wrong. I hope, at least, the BBC, which employs plenty of staff who understand video games, will make time in its schedule to take a good look at GTA VI – its themes and influences, its creators, its place in the wider culture of games and entertainment. Sure, arts coverage on BBC television has been in decline for years, with the broadcaster shifting this content to digital platforms, but I saw plenty of in-depth analysis of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, looking at the quality of its translation, its depiction of female characters, its use of practical effects. I didn’t see a single presenter shrugging, looking comedically bewildered and admitting they’d not read Homer since secondary school.

On top of this, whatever mainstream media attention GTA VI does get it will come at the expense of covering other titles. Because, when the next video game story comes up in the wake of Rockstar’s behemoth, TV and radio editors and producers will be thinking, “Oh, we covered games last month.”

The thing is, GTA is a phenomenon – it looks gorgeous, it looks vast, and it will sell many millions of copies. The series’ notoriety transcends the medium. But is it the most interesting video game since GTA V? So much has changed since then. We’ve explored the fascinating, innovative open worlds of Elden Ring, Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and No Man’s Sky (an open galaxy!); we’ve seen brutal adult themes explored in The Last of Us: Part 2 and Silent Hill; we’ve experienced dizzying narrative innovations via Disco Elysium, Split Fiction and Lost Records: Bloom & Rage. All of these deserved at least a portion of that GTA screen and radio time.

en.title: 'GTA 6' on PS5 vs Xbox: Key differences to consider
en.description: Grand Theft Auto VI launches on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles. As far as anyone knows, it could be years before there's a PC ve...
en.fullContent:
Grand Theft Auto VI launches on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles. As far as anyone knows, it could be years before there's a PC version of the hotly anticipated open-world crime game (fortunately, we don't think it will take that long). But if you want to play the game right away, then it's time for you to figure out which version to buy.

After pre-orders opened, IGN reported that PS5 versions of the game were outselling Xbox at an eight-to-one ratio. Microsoft denied these numbers, of course, but if IGN's readers are representative of gamers as a whole, then players are certainly leaning in a very clear direction.

So, should you play GTA 6 on PS5 or Xbox? There are a lot of variables that make this a difficult question to answer. That said, we're going to do our best. Here is everything you need to know before buying GTA VI on PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series S/X

The first thing to note here is that the only official gameplay footage we've seen of GTA 6 comes from a 26-minute extended look released on Netflix in late August. It lived up to the hype, but less than half an hour of carefully curated footage is not a great way to determine the technical ins and outs of a video game.

It's also worth pointing out, though, that the Netflix footage was captured on PlayStation 5. Sony has even said in its marketing that the game "plays best on PS5."

"Thanks to the close partnership between Sony Interactive Entertainment and Rockstar Games, Grand Theft Auto VI will play best on PS5 by taking advantage of PS5’s immersive features to deliver a deeply engaging single-player experience when it launches on November 19," a Sony blog post reads.

en.title: How Grand Theft Auto 6's visuals evolve over GTA 5 Enhanced
en.description: There's commonality, but the new game is a generation or two beyond.
en.fullContent:
There's commonality, but the new game is a generation or two beyond.

Grand Theft Auto 6's Extended Look was a revelation, representing a massive leap forward in visual fidelity and simulation, even when compared against its predecessor running in its ultimate iteration - the Enhanced Edition running on high-end PC with everything maxed. Fundamentally, we're looking at a step change here for the RAGE engine, as opposed to a game that received multiple iterations from launch but is fundamentally built from a foundation designed for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3.

One of the most noticeable differences lies in character rendering. GTA 5 characters still retain the same basic look as their 2013 launch counterparts with a waxy, plastic-like appearance that relies on normal mapping for fine detail, with subsurface scattering often struggling to replicate the particular look of human skin. In contrast, GTA 6 is on another level, with excellent diffuse and specular response, allowing for nuanced facial expressions. Clothing fidelity is clearly a generation apart too.

Hair technology is similarly enhanced. While GTA 5 displays hair as an undifferentiated mass, the new game uses strand-based hair for main characters and even for many NPCs. This allows for realistic movement, secondary animation and superior lighting diffusion. We may see distance-based reductions in fidelity in the fine game, but the GTA 6 achievement here is brilliant - not just a step beyond GTA 5 but pretty much every title we've seen in this generation too.

One area where there is little change is in animation update. The RAGE engine has a peculiar form of judder we've discussed in the past and it's been the engine for a long time - a GTA 5 artefact that made its way into Red Dead Redemption 2 and into GTA 6. It's as though the update in movement does not move in lock-step with the frame-rate. It's more obvious in GTA 5, but in the sequel, we've seen evidence of it in gameplay too, which is a first.

Lighting sees an interesting level of commonality between the GTA 5 Enhanced Edition and the new game as it appears that Rockstar used changes to the last game almost as a trial for ray tracing features in the upcoming title. High quality ray traced reflections are an impressive feature, but in GTA 5 they are ultimately constrained by the game's lack of a physically-based materials pipeline. Without a carefully authored roughness variation, materials can look rather uniform in GTA 5, so RT reflections don't look quite right. GTA 6 is state-of-the-art, built from the ground up with a modern PBR pipeline, so surfaces like dusty cars or rough concrete react accurately to light.
